analysis.one_liner: Caps federal farm subsidy payments to any one person and counts payments through partnerships and corporations.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in June 1990 and never received a committee hearing, floor vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal farm subsidy programs pay farmers for growing crops like wheat, cotton, and rice, but the law caps how much any one person can collect. Large operations get around those caps by splitting payments across partnerships, corporations, and family members. This bill would have counted payments by each real person's ownership share in any entity, capped most crop subsidy payments at $50,000 per person per year, capped total payments at $250,000, capped disaster payments at $100,000, and stopped a practice of redeeming government commodity certificates for cash.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would pay less in farm subsidies, and smaller family farms, which compete for federal support against very large operations that currently collect many times the per-person cap through layered entities. The bill would have limited payments for the 1991 through 1995 crops.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have required the Agriculture Department to attribute subsidy payments to natural persons in proportion to their ownership in corporations, partnerships, and other entities, closing a route large operations use to collect many separate payments.

It would have set a $50,000 per-person cap on deficiency and land diversion payments for the 1991 through 1995 crops, a $50,000 cap on related marketing loan gains and similar payments, and a $250,000 overall cap per person across all covered programs.

It would have capped disaster payments at $100,000 per person, capped wool and mohair program payments at $50,000, and barred Commodity Credit Corporation certificates from being redeemed for cash, limiting another channel for large payouts.

analysis.who_pays: Very large farm operations — principally producers of wheat, feed grains, cotton, and rice — that now collect subsidy payments far above the caps through multiple entities and family members. These operations would see federal payments reduced or restructured.

drawbacks.text: Payment caps can push very large operations to reorganize into more separate legal entities or reduce participation in the programs, which can blunt the intended savings and complicate administration for the Agriculture Department.

Caps do not distinguish between a large operation's size and its need; a producer with heavy planting costs and thin margins could lose support the programs were designed to provide, and some analysts argue broad caps can affect production decisions in major commodity crops.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward: fewer federal dollars flowing to the largest subsidy recipients through entity-splitting, and a fairer per-person limit for family-scale farms. The cost is real but modest — some very large operations would lose support or restructure to keep it, and the caps apply bluntly across operations of very different sizes. On balance this was a targeted integrity fix to farm programs, not a broad cut to farm support.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Silvio Conte introduced the bill on June 13, 1990, joined by Representatives Armey, Frank, Schumer, and Frenzel — a mix of Republicans and Democrats.
The bill had 10 cosponsors, six Republicans and four Democrats, showing support on both sides of the aisle.
The House Parliamentarian referred the bill to the House Committee on Agriculture on the day of introduction, and the action record shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote at any point afterward.
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, so the bill died in committee with the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Very large commodity farm operations that continued collecting payments above the per-person caps through partnerships and corporations, since no limitation was enacted. Taxpayers gained nothing because the savings were never realized.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large subsidy recipients; taxpayers gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Silvio Conte
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tighten per-person farm payment limitations and refer it to Agriculture.

for.name: Reps. Armey, Frank, Schumer, and Frenzel
for.role: Original cosponsors in the House (2 R, 2 D)
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction, making the bill bipartisan from day one.

for.name: 6 of 175 House Republicans and 4 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — six Republicans and four Democrats.

against.name: Rep. E. (Kika) de la Garza
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup; the bill shows no committee action after its June 1990 referral.

against.name: Large commodity farm operations
against.role: Recipients of federal crop subsidy payments
against.what_they_did: Large wheat, feed grain, cotton, and rice producers have historically opposed tightening payment limitations, which would reduce their federal receipts.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — a Republican sponsor joined by two Republican and two Democratic original cosponsors, and 10 cosponsors split six Republican and four Democratic — but no party ever brought the bill to a vote.

industries.industry: Large commodity farm operations (wheat, feed grains, cotton, rice)
industries.note: The bill would cap their subsidy collections at $50,000 per person per program and $250,000 overall, and would count payments through entities against each owner's share, directly reducing payments to the largest recipients. Their gain under current law is a cost to taxpayers and to smaller farms competing for the same programs.
The bill would cap National Wool Act payments at $50,000 per person for 1991 through 1995, trimming a program that pays producers based on wool and mohair sales.

industries.industry: Commodity certificate and marketing loan users
industries.note: The bill bars redeeming Commodity Credit Corporation certificates for cash and caps marketing loan gains at $50,000, closing channels large producers use to receive program benefits outside the nominal payment caps.
